es.summary: El ACV hemorrágico ocurre cuando un vaso cerebral se rompe, provocando sangrado dentro o alrededor del cerebro y aumento de la presión intracraneal.
key_points: Ruptura de vaso → sangrado intracraneal y aumento de presión intracraneal.
Hipertensión crónica es el factor de riesgo más frecuente.
Diagnóstico rápido con tomografía axial computarizada (TC) sin contraste.
Control estricto de la presión arterial y de la presión intracraneal es esencial.
Manejo quirúrgico según localización y volumen del hematoma.

pathophysiology: Ruptura de arteria cerebral por hipertensión, aneurisma o malformación.
El sangrado llena el parénquima o el espacio subaracnoideo, elevando la presión intracraneal.
Compresión del tejido cerebral reduce el flujo sanguíneo y causa isquemia secundaria.
El edema vasogénico y la herniación pueden desarrollarse en horas.
risk_factors: Consumo excesivo de alcohol y tabaquismo.
signs_symptoms: Dolor de cabeza súbito y severo (tipo “explosivo”).
Náuseas, vómitos y pérdida de conciencia.
diagnostics: TC cerebral sin contraste: hiperdensidad que indica sangre.
LCR: sangre en el líquido cefalorraquídeo si hay hemorragia subaracnoidea.
Hemograma: hemoglobina y hematocrito para evaluar pérdida sanguínea.
Presión arterial: mantener <140/90 mmHg; monitorizar continuamente.
treatment: Control de presión arterial con labetalol o nicardipina.
Reversión de anticoagulación: vitamina K, protamina, factor VIIa.
Manejo de presión intracraneal: manitol 20% o solución salina hipertónica.
Cirugía de evacuación de hematoma o clipado de aneurisma según indicación.
nursing_care: Evaluar nivel de conciencia con escala de Glasgow cada hora.
Monitorear presión arterial, frecuencia cardíaca y presión intracraneal.
Mantener posición semisentada (30°) para favorecer drenaje venoso.
Controlar equilibrio de líquidos y signos de hipovolemia.
Administrar medicamentos según prescripción y observar efectos adversos.
patient_teaching: Importancia de controlar la presión arterial en casa (≤140/90 mmHg).
Adherir al tratamiento anticoagulante o antihipertensivo según indicación.
Reconocer signos de alarma: dolor de cabeza intenso, visión borrosa, debilidad súbita.
Evitar esfuerzos físicos intensos y consumo de alcohol o tabaco.

care_plans.diagnosis: Riesgo de perfusión tisular cerebral ineficaz
outcomes: Mantener escala de Glasgow ≥ 15 durante 24 h
Presión arterial sistólica 100‑140 mmHg y diastólica <90 mmHg

interventions.action: Monitorear nivel de conciencia y escala de Glasgow cada hora
interventions.rationale: Detectar deterioro neurológico temprano permite intervención rápida.

interventions.action: Controlar presión arterial invasiva cada 15 min y ajustar antihipertensivos
interventions.rationale: Mantener presión arterial dentro del rango reduce expansión del hematoma.

interventions.action: Mantener posición semisentada (30°) y evitar maniobras que aumenten presión intracraneal
interventions.rationale: Facilita el drenaje venoso y disminuye la presión intracraneal.

interventions.action: Evaluar signos de aumento de presión intracraneal (pupilas, vómitos, hipertensión) y notificar al médico
interventions.rationale: La detección precoz permite medidas terapéuticas urgentes.

care_plans.diagnosis: Riesgo de déficit de volumen de líquidos

interventions.action: Registrar ingesta y salida de líquidos cada 2 h
interventions.rationale: Permite identificar desequilibrio de volumen rápidamente.

interventions.action: Monitorear signos vitales (PA, frecuencia cardíaca) y perfusión periférica
interventions.rationale: Indicadores tempranos de hipovolemia o sobrecarga.

interventions.action: Administrar soluciones cristaloides según prescripción y observar respuesta hemodinámica
interventions.rationale: Reemplaza el volumen perdido y mantiene perfusión cerebral.

interventions.action: Evaluar nivel de hemoglobina y hematocrito cada 12 h
interventions.rationale: Detecta anemia por sangrado y guía transfusión si es necesario.

interventions.action: Educar al paciente y familia sobre la importancia de reportar sangrado o vómitos persistentes
interventions.rationale: Facilita la detección precoz de pérdida adicional de volumen.

en.summary: Hemorrhagic stroke occurs when a cerebral vessel ruptures, causing bleeding inside or around the brain and increasing intracranial pressure.
key_points: Vessel rupture → intracranial bleeding and increased intracranial pressure.
Chronic hypertension is the most common risk factor.
Rapid diagnosis with non‑contrast computed tomography (CT).
Strict control of blood pressure and intracranial pressure is essential.
Surgical management based on location and hematoma volume.

pathophysiology: Rupture of a cerebral artery due to hypertension, aneurysm, or malformation.
Bleeding fills the parenchyma or subarachnoid space, raising intracranial pressure.
Compression of brain tissue reduces blood flow and causes secondary ischemia.
Vasogenic edema and herniation can develop within hours.
signs_symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, and loss of consciousness.
diagnostics: Non‑contrast brain CT: hyperdensity indicating blood.
CSF: blood in cerebrospinal fluid if subarachnoid hemorrhage present.
CBC: hemoglobin and hematocrit to assess blood loss.
Blood pressure: maintain <140/90 mmHg; continuous monitoring.
treatment: Blood pressure control with labetalol or nicardipine.
Reversal of anticoagulation: vitamin K, protamine, factor VIIa.
Intracranial pressure management: 20% mannitol or hypertonic saline.
Surgical evacuation of hematoma or aneurysm clipping as indicated.
nursing_care: Assess level of consciousness with Glasgow Coma Scale hourly.
Monitor blood pressure, heart rate, and intracranial pressure.
Maintain semi‑upright position (30°) to promote venous drainage.
Monitor fluid balance and signs of hypovolemia.
Administer medications per order and observe for adverse effects.
patient_teaching: Importance of home blood pressure control (≤140/90 mmHg).
Adhere to anticoagulant or antihypertensive therapy as prescribed.
Recognize alarm signs: intense headache, blurred vision, sudden weakness.
Avoid intense physical exertion and consumption of alcohol or tobacco.

care_plans.diagnosis: Risk for ineffective cerebral tissue perfusion
outcomes: Maintain Glasgow Coma Scale ≥15 for 24 h
Systolic blood pressure 100‑140 mmHg and diastolic <90 mmHg

interventions.action: Monitor level of consciousness and Glasgow Coma Scale hourly
interventions.rationale: Early detection of neurological decline allows prompt intervention.

interventions.action: Control invasive blood pressure every 15 min and adjust antihypertensives
interventions.rationale: Keeping blood pressure within range reduces hematoma expansion.

interventions.action: Maintain semi‑upright position (30°) and avoid maneuvers that increase intracranial pressure
interventions.rationale: Facilitates venous drainage and decreases intracranial pressure.

interventions.action: Assess signs of increased intracranial pressure (pupils, vomiting, hypertension) and notify the physician
interventions.rationale: Early detection permits urgent therapeutic measures.

interventions.action: Record intake and output every 2 h
interventions.rationale: Allows rapid identification of volume imbalance.

interventions.action: Monitor vital signs (BP, heart rate) and peripheral perfusion
interventions.rationale: Early indicators of hypovolemia or overload.

interventions.action: Administer crystalloid solutions per order and observe hemodynamic response
interventions.rationale: Replaces lost volume and maintains cerebral perfusion.

interventions.action: Assess hemoglobin and hematocrit every 12 h
interventions.rationale: Detects anemia from bleeding and guides transfusion if needed.

interventions.action: Educate patient and family on the importance of reporting persistent bleeding or vomiting
interventions.rationale: Facilitates early detection of additional volume loss.

sources.name: MedlinePlus en español: Accidente cerebrovascular hemorrágico

summary.0.quote: It occurs when a blood vessel in the brain bursts, causing bleeding (hemorrhage) in or around the brain. This bleeding increases pressure inside the skull and damages brain tissue.

key_points.0.quote: A hemorrhage is a bleed, which can be from a rupture or leak in a cerebral vessel, either within the brain or around the brain. Bleeding in either location can take up room in the finite space of the skull, causing increased cerebral pressure and cerebral edema.

sections.pathophysiology.1.quote: Bleeding in either location can take up room in the finite space of the skull, causing increased cerebral pressure and cerebral edema.

sections.risk_factors.1.quote: Cerebral trauma and bleeding from a brain tumor can cause ICH, as well as aneurysm ruptures and arteriovenous malformations.

sections.risk_factors.2.quote: Patients taking anticoagulants or antiplatelets are at risk for ICH because their blood is “thinner,” meaning that clotting times are increased.

sections.risk_factors.3.quote: Modifiable risk factors for hemorrhagic stroke are: hypertension smoking alcohol consumption antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy sympathomimetic drug usage

sections.signs_symptoms.0.quote: thunderclap headache , a severe, sudden headache that peaks in intensity in seconds, lasts at least five minutes, and lingers and fades within a few hours

sections.signs_symptoms.1.quote: These include: decreased level of consciousness or coma thunderclap headache , a severe, sudden headache that peaks in intensity in seconds, lasts at least five minutes, and lingers and fades within a few hours vomiting seizure activity neck stiffness or pain

sections.diagnostics.0.quote: A head CT is the first imaging done in response to the signs and symptoms of a stroke because it determines whether a bleed is present, dictating the course of treatment.

sections.diagnostics.3.quote: The systolic goal is < 160–180 mmHg for patients who have received tPA, but it may be even higher (up to 220/120) for those who did not receive tPA.

sections.treatment.0.quote: Control within these parameters may require intravenous administration of labetalol or nicardipine.

sections.treatment.3.quote: Surgical interventions for hemorrhagic stroke aim to stop bleeding, aspirate the hematoma, or relieve pressure on the brain.

sections.complications.1.quote: Fisher scale Modified Fisher scale To index risk for vasospasm and delayed cerebral ischemia related to vasospasm after SAH

sections.patient_teaching.2.quote: Sudden severe headache with no known cause
